_note: Every fact the game states lives here, with a source and an honest note about what was simplified. Teachers: the 'simplification' field is the grown-up version. source.verified=false means the link could not be opened from the build environment and must be checked by a person before release (see README > Release checklist).

facts.title: Gravity fades with distance
facts.text: Twice as far from a planet, its gravity pulls only a quarter as hard. That's the inverse-square law Isaac Newton described.
facts.simplification: The game uses Newton's law with scaled-down masses and distances, and a tiny 'softening' term so gravity never becomes infinite at a point.

facts.title: Orbits are falling
facts.text: Astronauts float because they and their station are falling around Earth together, moving sideways so fast that they keep missing the ground.

source.title: NASA Science: Basics of Space Flight, Orbital Mechanics

facts.simplification: Game orbits are flat (2D). Real orbits are 3D and slightly disturbed by other bodies.

facts.title: Free speed from planets
facts.text: Voyager 2 used flybys of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune to gain speed and change direction. It's now in interstellar space.
facts.simplification: In the game the moon's speed is shown exaggerated so the effect is easy to feel.

facts.title: The iridium clue
facts.text: In 1980, scientists found a thin clay layer rich in iridium all over Earth. It helped show that an asteroid impact about 66 million years ago played a key part in the dinosaurs' extinction.
facts.simplification: Volcanic eruptions in India (the Deccan Traps) may also have played a role; scientists still discuss the details.

facts.title: Deeper is older
facts.text: In undisturbed rock, each layer is younger than the one below it. Geologists call this the law of superposition.
facts.simplification: Folding and faulting can flip real rock layers; the game's layers are undisturbed.

facts.title: Venus, the oven planet
facts.text: Venus's air is about 96% carbon dioxide. Its surface is hotter than Mercury's, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
facts.simplification: Veil is a made-up world inspired by Venus.

facts.title: Stars brighten as they age
facts.text: Sun-like stars slowly brighten. Our young Sun shone about 30% dimmer than it does today.
facts.simplification: The FORGE time-lapse uses a simple 'about 10% brighter per billion years' rule.

facts.title: The Goldilocks zone
facts.text: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet could have liquid water on its surface. Not too hot, not too cold.
facts.simplification: Zone edges use a simple formula based on the star's brightness; real zones also depend on each planet's air.

facts.title: Braking with air
facts.text: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter dipped into Mars's upper atmosphere hundreds of times in 2006 to slow down and shrink its orbit without using much fuel.
facts.simplification: The game squeezes many careful passes into one dramatic skim.

facts.title: The two-burn trick
facts.text: The Hohmann transfer, described by Walter Hohmann in 1925, moves a spacecraft between two circular orbits with two engine burns, using very little fuel.

source.title: NASA Science: Basics of Space Flight, Interplanetary Trajectories

facts.simplification: Game burns happen instantly; real engines burn for minutes.

facts.title: Calm spots in space
facts.text: Lagrange points are places where a small object can keep pace with a planet. The James Webb Space Telescope orbits near one of them (Sun–Earth L2), and Jupiter has thousands of 'Trojan' asteroids at its L4 and L5 points.

source.title: NASA Science: What is a Lagrange Point?

facts.simplification: The game shows L4, which is stable when the planet is much lighter than its star.

facts.title: Black holes
facts.text: Inside a black hole's event horizon, gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. We spot them by the X-rays from hot gas swirling in, and by how they tug on nearby stars.
facts.simplification: The game uses ordinary Newtonian gravity right up to the horizon; real black holes need Einstein's general relativity.

facts.title: Escape velocity
facts.text: To leave Earth for good without more pushing, you'd need about 11.2 km/s. That's over 30 times the speed of sound!
facts.simplification: Game speeds are scaled down to fit the screen.

facts.title: Starlight is old news
facts.text: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach us, and from the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 years. We see stars as they were when the light left.
facts.simplification: The Orrin system's 38 light-year distance is invented.

facts.title: Pulsars
facts.text: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars that sweep beams across space like lighthouses. Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered the first one in 1967. The Crab pulsar spins about 30 times a second.
facts.simplification: The game shows pulse timing only, not the radio telescope data astronomers use.

facts.title: Planet hunting with shadows
facts.text: When a planet passes in front of its star, the starlight dips a tiny bit. Most known exoplanets were found this way, by missions like Kepler and TESS.

source.title: NASA Science: Exoplanets, ways to find a planet

facts.simplification: Real dips are often far smaller than 1%; the game makes them easier to see.

facts.title: Counting in primes
facts.text: In 1974 the Arecibo telescope beamed a message to space. It had 1,679 bits, which is 23 × 73, two primes, so aliens could arrange it into a picture.
facts.simplification: The Orrin glyphs are invented, inspired by this idea.

facts.title: Iron stops the furnace
facts.text: Stars make energy by fusing light elements into heavier ones. That works all the way up to iron, but fusing iron uses up energy. In a massive star, the iron core collapses and the star explodes as a supernova.
facts.simplification: Real stars don't get ingredients poured in! A star's mass mostly decides its fate.

facts.title: Big stars live fast
facts.text: Massive blue stars burn out in a few million years. Small red dwarfs can shine for trillions of years, longer than the universe has existed so far.
facts.simplification: The game uses the rule lifetime ≈ 10 billion years × mass^-2.5.

facts.title: Red giants
facts.text: When a Sun-like star runs low on hydrogen in its core, it swells into a red giant, then sheds its outer layers and leaves a white dwarf.
facts.simplification: The game's time-lapse skips the detailed stages.

facts.title: Our Sun's long future
facts.text: Our Sun is about halfway through its life. In roughly 5 billion years it will become a red giant. Modern humans have been around for about 300,000 years.
facts.simplification: Scientists also estimate Earth may get too warm for oceans in about a billion years, still an enormous span of time.

facts.title: Space weather
facts.text: Solar flares are bursts of light and radiation. Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are huge clouds of charged gas that can shake Earth's magnetic field and damage satellites.
facts.simplification: In the game a CME gives the ship a gentle shove; a real one wouldn't noticeably push a heavy spacecraft.

facts.title: Planet-wide dust storms
facts.text: In 2018 a dust storm covered all of Mars and blocked so much sunlight that the solar-powered Opportunity rover went silent.
facts.simplification: Cinder's storms are shorter than real Martian ones.

facts.title: Why the Moon has phases
facts.text: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. Phases come from how much of that lit half we see from Earth, not from Earth's shadow.
facts.simplification: The game's moon-phase calculation can be off by a few hours.
